newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Tutsi fighters take east Zaire town, refugees flee.
newsitem.headline: Tutsi fighters take east Zaire town, refugees flee.

text.p: Ethnic Tutsis fighting Zairean troops in eastern Zaire were reported to have seized a town just miles away from hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees who will move if pushed, aid workers in Geneva said on Saturday.
If confirmed, the capture of the town of Rutshuru, only 10 km (six miles) away from sprawling refugee camps home to 700,000 Hutus, could set off another big exodus of refugees, they said.

In Uvira and Bukavu regions further to the south, the U.N. says 300,000 Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees are on the run, fleeing clashes between Zairean troops and Banyamulenge Tutsis who came to Zaire as long ago as the end of the 18th century and are resisting Zairean attempts to force them back to Rwanda.
Military sources and state radio in Burundi said on Saturday that Tutsi fighters had seized the town of Uvira after two days of clashes with Zairean troops.

There have been no credible witness accounts of the fighting so far, but reports of the lightning Tutsi guerrilla advance in Uvira and Bukavu to the south and Goma to the north could indicate a two-pronged, coordinated attack, aid officials said.
In Goma, reports from aid workers described Rutshuru as "a war zone".
A spokesman for the U.N. refugee agency in Geneva said more than 20 Rwandan Hutu refugees were wounded on Saturday in an attack by gunmen on Kibumba camp, home to 190,000 people, in Goma.

Spokesman Francis Kpatinde said the UNHCR would evacuate 32 non-essential expatriate staff in Goma. In Bukavu too, nearly 100 U.N. expatriate staff including UNHCR employees would be evacuated on Saturday, he told Reuters.
The camps in Goma, sprawling tent cities where enterprising Hutus have set up cinemas, restaurants, brothels, hotels, post offices and churches, are next to Rwanda's mountainous borders.

Rutshuru is near yet another conflict zone in eastern Zaire, Masisi region, where native Zairean tribes aided by Hutus are warring ethnic Tutsis. Hundreds of Zairean Tutsis were killed in attacks by Hutus and Zairean troops in Masisi in recent months.
Aid workers said they expected the Tutsi guerrillas to try to empty the camps in Goma and force the Hutus away from Rwanda's borders.

The Rwandan refugees, costing the world $1 million a day in aid, fled in fear of reprisal for 1994's Hutu-led genocide of Tutsis. Many killed or watched others kill and refuse to return home where Tutsis swept to power after the genocide.

Rwanda's minority Tutsi rulers, who feel persecuted, outnumbered and surrounded by majority Hutus, have repeatedly asked the U.N. to close down the camps where Hutu militia stage frequent raids into Rwanda.
"If Rutshuru has fallen, the refugees have only two places to go -- back into Rwanda or into Masisi," said a Western aid worker from the region currently in Geneva.

U.N. officials in Geneva said they were making emergency plans in case of a possible influx of refugees into Rwanda, where genocide wounds are still festering and hundreds of Hutus have been killed in reprisal attacks by Tutsis.
The Tutsi resistance in eastern Zaire appears more coordinated in recent days and Zaire has accused Rwanda of invading. Rwanda has denied the charge.

But some members of Rwanda's Tutsi-led army say privately they are prepared to take matters into their own hands. Many of the army's soldiers grew up in neighbouring Zaire, Uganda and Burundi and would be at home across the borders.
